## In this lab {#plan}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## The privacy line
No patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop. Case cards only.
:::

::: notes
**Before the clock starts.** Lab Two is one case, three readers. Part 1, twenty minutes: build one sheet from a case card, check it, draw a chart note, a patient handout and three slides from it, then fill in the grid. Part 2, ten minutes: Day One's tool comparison again, on a Day Two task. Part 3, five minutes: a share-out where we apply the three-question check together. The privacy line applies to every prompt you paste.

**Do.** Paste the lab page link in the chat. You keep the time: call each clock cue aloud and type it in the chat.
:::

## Have these open before the clock starts {#setup}

- Your general assistant, and your second option from Lab One ([Module 3](../day1/m3-choosing-tools.qmd#second-option))
- [Case A](../reference/case-cards.qmd#case-a), or any [case card](../reference/case-cards.qmd)
- The [prompt library](../reference/prompt-library.qmd)
- A notes app, for the two grids

This deck keeps the time. The workspace is the [lab page](../day2/lab2-one-case-three-outputs.qmd): keep the lab page open in another window.

::: notes
**Before the clock starts.** Give people a minute to open these. Case A is the default because its card is written for exactly these three outputs; any card is allowed. Anyone without a tool yet follows your shared screen for the sheet and one output. If a tool misbehaves, point them to the troubleshooting page. This deck is the clock; the lab page is the workspace.

**Do.** Chat, thirty seconds: everyone types "ready" when their tabs are open. Start part 1 when most have typed it.
:::

# Part 1: One case, three outputs [20 min]{.time} {#part-1}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone leaves part 1 with a sheet they checked, a chart note, a patient handout and a three-slide teaching version made from it, and a grid showing whether the three agree.

**Have ready.** Case A, and your own full run of part 1 with the grid filled in, so you know what a mismatch looks like. A saved backup set to share on screen if a tool goes down. The lab page link in the chat.

**Clock.** Minutes 0 to 4, the sheet. 4 to 14, the three outputs: at 4 "new chat for each output", at 9 "second output by now", at 12 "take what you have and move on". 14 to 20, the grid.

**Watch for.** Skipping the sheet check to reach the outputs faster: the commonest failure. Judging by fluency: "this one reads better". A grid full of ok that nobody looked at.

**If asked.** Why a new chat for each output? An error in one cannot leak into the next, and each draws on the sheet, not on the others. Can I use my own case? A card is safer; if you do, apply the privacy checklist first.

**Bridge.** "Same comparison as Day One, new task: compare what you can see, not which answer sounded better."
:::

## Step 1: Build the sheet, then fix it {#p1-sheet}

[Prompt library: source-of-truth-sheet](../reference/prompt-library.qmd#p-source-of-truth-sheet), run on your card's bullets.

Then check the sheet against the card, line by line: **invented**, **omitted**, **altered**. Fix it by hand.

An error left here is copied into all three outputs. [Lab page, part 1](../day2/lab2-one-case-three-outputs.qmd#part-1).

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 4 min]{.tag} Build the sheet, then check it against the card.
:::

::: notes
**4:00.** One case, three readers, one sheet. Build the sheet and fix it yourself before anything else. No patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop. Cards only. Then check the sheet against the card line by line for invented, omitted, altered. This step decides everything after it: an error left in the sheet is copied into all three outputs. It is the verification workflow one level up, with the card as the source.

**Do.** Solo. Watch the chat and answer questions there. Near minute 3, ask everyone to type "sheet checked" as they finish; do not move on while many are still reading. At minute 4 say: new chat for each output.
:::

Paste the sheet into each chat. Change only the placeholders. [Lab page, part 1](../day2/lab2-one-case-three-outputs.qmd#part-1).

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 10 min]{.tag} About three minutes each. If one runs long, take what you have and move on.

::: notes
**10:00.** A new chat for each output, with the sheet pasted into each one: an error in one cannot leak into the next, and each draws on the sheet, not on the others. Paste each prompt as taught and change only its placeholders, plus any setting words that do not fit your case, such as a clinic visit instead of an operation. For the slides, the three titles to type under OUTLINE are on the lab page. About three minutes per output. The check in step 3 is the point of the lab.

**Do.** Solo. Cues by the part clock: at 9, "second output by now"; at 12, "take what you have and move on". Watch the chat for stuck tools; share your saved backup set for anyone without a working tool.
:::

## Step 3: Do the three outputs agree? {#p1-grid}

Mark each constant fact in each output: **ok**, **altered**, **omitted** or **n/a**. The last row is **invented**.

If two outputs disagree, the sheet and the card decide, not whichever output reads better. [Lab page, part 1](../day2/lab2-one-case-three-outputs.qmd#part-1).

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 5 min]{.tag} Fill in the grid on the lab page. Every cell gets a mark.
:::

::: notes
**5:00.** Now find out whether the three outputs agree. For each constant fact, find it in each output and mark the cell: ok, altered, omitted, or n/a when it was left out on purpose. The last row is invented. If two outputs disagree, go to the sheet and the card, not to whichever output reads better, then ask whether the sheet itself was the source. Case A names no warning signs to return for: a handout that lists some did not get them from the card.

**Do.** Solo. Share the Module 4 consistency check slide for a minute as the model. Early finishers: another card through the same three prompts, or a handout in Arabic for Case C or D, which a fluent Arabic reader must check.
:::

## Part 1: what good looks like {#p1-good}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[01]{.num}

The sheet was fixed before any output existed.
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[02]{.num}

Doses, intervals and readings are identical everywhere, copied from the sheet.
:::
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[03]{.num}

Where the card is silent: [MISSING: ...] or nothing.
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[04]{.num}

Every grid cell is marked. A clean grid is fine if you checked.
:::
:::

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 30 sec]{.tag} Type what your grid found: mismatch, extra content, or clean.
:::

::: notes
**1:00.** Check yourself against these four: the sheet fixed before any output existed; every dose, interval and reading identical wherever it appears, copied from the sheet; where the card is silent, MISSING or nothing, never a filled gap; every grid cell marked. A grid with no mismatch is a good result if you checked; a grid nobody filled in is not. If the chat has room: which fact was hardest to keep still across the three outputs?

**Do.** Chat, thirty seconds: type what your grid found. Pick three volunteers for part 3 from the answers: one mismatch, one whose handout added content, one clean. Ask each by name in the chat to be ready to share. Leave them with the line: one sheet, three outputs, one grid; an output that disagrees with the sheet is wrong, however fluent it sounds. Then the bridge from the topic slide.
:::

# Part 2: Tool check, again [10 min]{.time} {#part-2}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone repeats Day One's comparison on a Day Two task and says what held and what did not, from what they could see.

**Have ready.** The practice source open in a tab, the study-summary prompt in your assistant, and a saved run to share on screen. The lab page link in the chat.

**Clock.** Minute 0 to 1, choose the task and copy the source. 1 to 5, run the prompt in both. 5 to 9, the table. 9 to 10, the two closing lines.

**Watch for.** Part 2 turning into a brand debate: point at the table. Judging by fluency: "this one reads better". A tool that will not take the pasted text, or answers from its own sources: they write it down; that is a result, not a failure.

**If asked.** Which tool won? That is not the result: the four questions in the table are. Which task? The default is the study summary; the Case C referral letter is the other option, on the lab page.

**Bridge.** "Last five minutes: do together what you have been doing alone. Pick the one output you would least want to be wrong."
:::

::: {.card}
[The task]{.t} A study summary from the [practice source](../reference/practice-source.qmd). [Prompt library: teaching-summary-from-source](../reference/prompt-library.qmd#p-teaching-summary-from-source)
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[If your second option cannot take pasted text]{.t} Ask both for the evidence behind one number, such as 135/85.
:::
:::

[Lab page, part 2](../day2/lab2-one-case-three-outputs.qmd#part-2)

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 5 min]{.tag} Paste the same prompt, unchanged, into both tools. A tool that will not take your text? Write it down.
:::

::: notes
**5:00.** Same comparison as Day One, new task. The default is a study summary from the practice source; the Case C referral letter with the Day One referral prompt is the alternative, on the lab page. Paste the same prompt, unchanged, into both tools. If the second option cannot take pasted text, as a plain literature search cannot, ask both for the evidence behind one number in the practice source, such as the 135/85 threshold, and compare what each lets you check. A tool that will not take your text, or answers from its own sources, gives you a result: write it down.

**Do.** Solo. At minute 1 say: "task chosen, source copied, now run it in both". At minute 4 say: "take what you have; the table is next". Watch the chat for stuck tools; share your saved run for anyone without one.
:::

## Compare what you can see {#p2-compare}

The table on the lab page asks what each tool stayed inside, added, cited and copied exactly.

[Not which one sounded better.]{.big}

If a tool cited something, open it before you believe it. [Lab page, part 2](../day2/lab2-one-case-three-outputs.qmd#part-2).

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 4 min]{.tag} Fill in the table.
:::

::: notes
**4:00.** Compare what you can see, not which answer sounded better. The table asks four things: did it stay inside the text, did it add anything that is not in it, did it cite something and could you open it, and did it copy every number exactly. If a tool cited something, open it before you believe it. The two lines under the table come in the last minute.

**Do.** Solo. At minute 8 of the part, say: one minute left on the table. Watch the chat and answer questions there. If the group drifts into which tool is better, point at the table.
:::

## Part 2: what good looks like {#p2-good}

- You compared what you can see, not which answer sounded better.
- You opened any citation before you believed it.
- Your "because" names something you observed.

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 1 min]{.tag} Finish the two lines under the table: did the Day One pattern hold, and which tool you would use for this job.
:::

::: notes
**1:00.** Finish the two lines under the table: did the Day One pattern hold, and which tool you would use for this job, and why. Good looks like this. You compared on things you can see. If a tool cited something, you opened it. Your because names something you observed, not a feeling about the tool. If the chat has room, ask what the second tool did differently and what you would use each for.

**Do.** Solo for the two lines. Read out two "because" lines from the chat if people post them. Leave them with the line: same task, two ways of answering; compare what each stayed inside, added and cited. Which one sounded better is not a result. Then the bridge from the topic slide.
:::

# Part 3: Share-out [5 min]{.time} {#part-3}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone applies the three-question check to an output someone else made: the move they will need when a colleague hands them an AI-drafted note and asks if it looks fine.

**Have ready.** Your three volunteers from part 1: one with a mismatch, one whose handout added content, one clean. A saved backup output to share if nobody can. The three questions are on the slides.

**Clock.** Minute 0 to 1, everyone picks the output they would least want to be wrong. 1 to 4, two or three volunteers share. 4 to 5, everyone writes one thing to change.

**Watch for.** "It looked fine" instead of a named fact and where it was checked. A "no" with no next step. The group questioning the person, not the output. Losing this part: protect these five minutes and shorten part 2 instead.

**If asked.** What if my answer to a question is no? That is a good answer here. What matters is what you do next: check the source, or delete the line.

**Bridge.** "Tomorrow is Day Three: what goes wrong, and what never goes in. Have ready the Lab One output you saved, which Lab Three uses, and one output from today, which the session Back to the rule uses."
:::

## Pick one output {#p3-pick}

[The one you would least want to be wrong.]{.big}

The patient handout is a good candidate: a patient will act on it. Put it beside its sheet.

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 1 min]{.tag} Choose it and put it beside its sheet. Volunteers: have your screen ready to share.
:::

::: notes
**1:00.** The last five minutes are for doing together what you have been doing alone: applying the check to something a colleague made. It is the same move you will need at work, when someone hands you an AI-drafted note and asks whether it looks fine. Pick the one output you would least want to be wrong. The patient handout is a good candidate, because a patient will act on it.

**Do.** Solo for a minute. Ask your three volunteers, by name in the chat, to have their screen ready. If one is missing, take another from the chat answers in part 1.
:::

Everyone answers the three questions in the chat for that output: could I defend this to a colleague, does it point to something I can verify, would I catch it if it were wrong. :::

## Part 3: what good looks like {#p3-good}

If the answer to any of these is no, that's the signal to slow down, not the finding to accept.

- The volunteer names a specific fact and where they checked it.
- A "no" comes with a next step.

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 1 min]{.tag} Write one thing you will change next time, in the sheet or in the prompt.
:::

::: notes
**1:00.** What good looks like: the volunteer names a specific fact and where they checked it, not "it looked fine". A no comes with a next step: check the source, or delete the line. Everyone questions the output, not the person. Then each person writes one thing to change next time, in the sheet or in the prompt. If time allows, ask which output you would send without one more read; the rule expects none.

**Do.** Solo for the last minute. Read out two or three changes if people post them in the chat. Leave them with the line: fluent is not verified; say what you checked, against what, and what you would still check. Then the bridge from the topic slide: Day Three tomorrow, and what to have ready.
:::

## If it goes wrong {#fixes}

| Problem | Fix |
|----------|---------------------|
| A real case turns up | Stop and use a card. Already pasted something? Follow the [privacy checklist](../reference/privacy-checklist.qmd). |
| Tool slow, or quota gone | Switch to your other tool, or follow the trainer's shared backup set. Never use anyone else's login. |
| The sheet is prose, or longer than the card | Facts only, one per line. |
| The handout lists warning signs | Case A names none. Delete the list, or write your own. |
| Two outputs disagree | The sheet and the card decide. Fix the sheet, then rerun that output in a new chat. |
| A tool will not take your text | Write it down. That is a result, not a failure. |

::: notes
**On demand, no clock.** Keep this slide for when something goes wrong; do not present it. Answer in the chat with the row that fits. A real case is the one to stop for: say it without blame, send them to a card, and point to the privacy checklist for what to do next; Day Three covers why. A slow tool is not a failure of the lab: the sheet and two outputs are enough, then follow your backup set on screen.

**Do.** Chat the fix; do not read the table aloud. If the problem is a participant's call setup, the troubleshooting page covers it.
:::
